evidence: Cic. Off. 1.30: quod dubitēs aequum sit an inīquum
terms.comment: With a question (utrum … an, -ne … an, num), with dē and the ablative, or with a neuter pronoun. “I have no doubt that” is nōn dubitō quīn with the subjunctive (Lewis & Short), or nōn mihi dubium est quīn (Traupman 97, 306); an accusative and infinitive comes in only with Nepos and Livy, and then after a negative (Lewis & Short). On its own, dubitō an, like haud sciō an, leans to yes, “I rather think” (Lewis & Short, s.v. an). With an infinitive, dubitō is “hesitate” (Cic. Sen. 25).

terms.gloss: doubt: sine dubiō, no doubt; in dubium vocāre, call in question
evidence: Sen. Ep. 53.1: erat sine dubiō caelum grave
Cic. de Or. 2.145: quae in dubium vocārentur
terms.comment: The neuter of dubius, doubtful; haud dubiē, undoubtedly, is the word of Sallust and Livy (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: quōcircā bene praecipiunt quī vetant quicquam agere quod dubitēs aequum sit an inīquum
phrases.english: so they advise well who forbid us to do anything when we are in doubt whether it is fair or unfair

phrases.latin: neque enim dubitārī potest, quīn artis pars magna contineātur imitātiōne
phrases.english: for there can be no doubt that a great part of any art lies in imitation
O you of little faith, why did you doubt?
